A_target.statement:
Let $R$ be a [[Definition:Well-Founded Relation|well-founded relation]] on a set $A$ and $G$ a rule assigning a value to each $a \in A$ given values on its $R$-predecessors.
Then there exists a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] $F$ on $A$ such that:
:$\forall a \in A: \map F a = \map G {a, F \restriction_{\set {b: b \mathrel R a} } }$

B_source.statement:
Let $c$ be given and $g$ a function.
Then there is a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] $f: \N \to X$ with $\map f 0 = c$ and $\map f {n + 1} = \map g {\map f n}$.

substitutions.the predecessor of a natural number: the set of all R-predecessors of an element
substitutions.the induction along the usual order: induction along the well-founded relation R
substitutions.the base case at zero: the R-minimal elements, which have no predecessors

derived.the argument by induction on n: the argument by well-founded induction on R

validity_conditions: Well-foundedness is exactly the hypothesis that makes the induction step legitimate, since it rules out infinite descending chains.
The base case needs no separate treatment: R-minimal elements have empty predecessor sets, so the recursion clause determines their values outright.
Uniqueness is proved by well-founded induction on the set where two candidate solutions could differ, which must be empty since it has no R-minimal element.
proof_plan: Replace the predecessor $n$ of $n + 1$ by the set $\set {b: b \mathrel R a}$ of $R$-predecessors of $a$.

Call $h$ an approximation if its domain is $R$-downward closed and it satisfies the recursion on its domain.
By [[Principle of Well-Founded Induction|well-founded induction]], any two approximations agree on the intersection of their domains.

Let $F$ be the union of all approximations.
$F$ is a function, and if some $a$ were outside its domain, an $R$-minimal such $a$ could be added, contradicting maximality.
Hence $F$ is total and satisfies the recursion.
